classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish intersections from inclusive unions, use the supplied definition of court cards, and subtract the Club–court overlap while recognising disjoint groups in other parts.

content.prompt: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of playing cards. Find the probability that the card chosen:

answer.worked:
There are 13 Clubs in the 52-card pack.
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{Club})&=\frac{13}{52}\\P(\text{Club})&=\frac{1}{4}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: is a court card (that is, Ace, King, Queen or Jack)

answer.worked:
Using the question's definition, there are $4\times4=16$ court cards.
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{court card})&=\frac{16}{52}\\P(\text{court card})&=\frac{4}{13}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: has a face value between 2 and 9 inclusive

answer.worked:
There are eight values, $2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9$, in each of four suits: $8\times4=32$ cards.
$$\begin{align*}P(2\text{ to }9)&=\frac{32}{52}\\P(2\text{ to }9)&=\frac{8}{13}\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: is a Club and a court card

answer.worked:
The intersection contains the Ace, King, Queen and Jack of Clubs: four cards.
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{Club}\cap\text{court card})&=\frac{4}{52}\\P(\text{Club}\cap\text{court card})&=\frac{1}{13}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: is a Club or a court card

answer.short:
$\frac{25}{52}$

Count the union, subtracting the four court cards that are Clubs once.
answer.worked:
There are 13 Clubs, 16 court cards and four cards in both groups. By the addition rule,
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{Club}\cup\text{court card})&=\frac{13}{52}+\frac{16}{52}-\frac{4}{52}\\P(\text{Club}\cup\text{court card})&=\frac{25}{52}\end{align*}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: has a face value between 2 and 5 inclusive and is a court card

answer.worked:
No card with value 2, 3, 4 or 5 is an Ace, King, Queen or Jack. The events are mutually exclusive.
$$P((2\text{ to }5)\cap\text{court card})=0$$

children.label: g
children.prompt: has a face value between 2 and 5 inclusive or is a court card

answer.short:
$\frac{8}{13}$

Add the probabilities of the two mutually exclusive groups.
answer.worked:
There are $4\times4=16$ cards with values 2 to 5 and 16 court cards. These groups have no cards in common.
$$\begin{align*}P((2\text{ to }5)\cup\text{court card})&=\frac{16}{52}+\frac{16}{52}\\P((2\text{ to }5)\cup\text{court card})&=\frac{32}{52}\\P((2\text{ to }5)\cup\text{court card})&=\frac{8}{13}\end{align*}$$
